content:
In the following code, both ChatGPT and Gemini tell me that the theorem I want to prove is not true. Is that really the case? I was able to define recursive functions on VTree (see the function paths below). How does Lean prove the termination of paths?

inductive VTree (α : Type*)
  | node (val : α) (knum : ℕ) (kmap : Fin knum → VTree α) : VTree α

namespace VTree

variable {α : Type*}

abbrev val : VTree α → α
  | node val _ _ => val

abbrev kids : VTree α → List (VTree α)
  | node _ _ kmap => List.ofFn kmap

abbrev mk (val : α) (kids : List (VTree α)) : VTree α :=
  node val kids.length (kids.get ·)

theorem sizeOf_kid {t k : VTree α} (h : k ∈ t.kids) : sizeOf k < sizeOf t := by
  sorry

def paths : VTree α → Finset (List ℕ)
  | node _ knum kmap =>
    let kidsPaths (k : ℕ) := if hk : k < knum then (paths (kmap ⟨k, hk⟩)).image (k :: ·) else ∅
    Finset.biUnion (range knum) kidsPaths

end VTree

I should provide some context for the above question. Originally I started with a nested inductive definition for VTree. But at present Lean does know how to do induction on such definitions, which is why I ended up with the definition above:
#CSLib > New library dependency

The kind of termination that it uses in paths is simply structural termination, it doesn't ever use sizeOf. And yes, the theorem is false because it simply ignores kmap in the size calculation. The SizeOf deriving handler doesn't handle reflexive occurrences (i.e. recursive occurrences of the inductive type within a function type) so they don't become part of the sizeOf t. If you want a counterexample:

theorem sizeOf_kid {t k : VTree α} (h : k ∈ t.kids) : sizeOf k < sizeOf t := by
  impossible by
  intro h
  let node1 : VTree PUnit := .node ⟨⟩ 0 nofun
  let node2 : VTree PUnit := .node ⟨⟩ 2 ![node1, node1]
  let node3 : VTree PUnit := .node ⟨⟩ 1 ![node2]
  specialize @h PUnit node3 node2
  rw [List.mem_ofFn] at h
  specialize h ⟨0, rfl⟩
  conv_lhs at h => simp +zetaDelta
  conv_rhs at h => simp +zetaDelta
  contradiction

But I would like to make recursive definitions on VTree in terms of VTree.kids, I guess I will have to define my own size functions like the following and then use well-founded recursion. Correct? Is there a better method?

def size : VTree α → ℕ
  | node val knum kmap =>
    let kidsSizes := univ.image (fun k ↦ size (kmap k))
    let kidsMax := if h : kidsSizes.Nonempty then kidsSizes.max' h else 0
    1 + sizeOf val + sizeOf knum + kidsMax

Using a nested inductive type?

import Mathlib

structure VTree (α : Type*) where
  val : α
  kids : List (VTree α)

namespace VTree

variable {α : Type*}

def paths : VTree α → Finset (List ℕ)
  | { kids := kids, .. } =>
    let kidsPaths (k : Fin kids.length) := (paths kids[k.val]).image (k.val :: ·)
    Finset.biUnion (Finset.univ : Finset <| Fin kids.length) kidsPaths
termination_by x => x
decreasing_by simp; grind [→ List.sizeOf_lt_of_mem, List.getElem_mem]

end VTree

And if you need an induction principle, here you go:

@[elab_as_elim, induction_eliminator]
def induction {α : Type u} {motive : VTree α → Sort v}
    (mk : ∀ val kids, (∀ x ∈ kids, motive x) → motive (mk val kids))
    (t : VTree α) : motive t :=
  match t with
  | { val, kids } => mk val kids fun x _ => @induction α motive mk x

Thanks! Alas, where are these things explained in various Lean educational materials? At the end of chapter 7 of #tpil, there is this example:

inductive Tree (α : Type u) where
  | mk : α → List (Tree α) → Tree α

But when I try to do induction on Tree, Lean says it can't do it because of the nested inductive definition. (#tpil provides no example about how to reason about the above definition.) And I didn't know an induction principle can be defined. I had always thought it needed to be proved somehow. Which is why I had my verion of VTree above, because Lean lets me do induction on it, which allows me to prove my induction principle.

Nor have I seen any example of using structure to define an inductive type. Is this documented somewhere? In fact, #tpil gives the strong impression that structure is used for non-recursive inductive types. For example, read the second paragraph at the beginning of chapter 9.

Well, for nested inductive types it's usually simpler to use recursion instead of induction (at least without having written a custom induction principle). It's often also case without nested inductives because recursion has good support and can do a lot more than induction. If you're referring to the fact that I wrote a def here and not a theorem well that's just because I can do it without any more effort. Of course, I could've just written a recursive theorem instead.

Also, yes, it used to be the case that structures need to be non-recursive but that was changed in lean4#5783 on Halloween 2024. However, that paragraph was written in 2021, where structures needed to be non-recursive.

Also, it's not like you can't use induction; it's just more awkward since you have to specify motives manually:

@[elab_as_elim, induction_eliminator]
theorem induction {α : Type u} {motive : VTree α → Prop}
    (mk : ∀ val kids, (∀ x ∈ kids, motive x) → motive (mk val kids))
    (t : VTree α) : motive t := by
  induction t using @VTree.rec (motive_2 := fun l : List (VTree α) => ∀ x ∈ l, motive x) with
  | mk val kids ih => exact mk val kids ih
  | nil x hxmem => nomatch hxmem
  | cons head tail head_ih tail_ih x hxmem =>
    rw [List.mem_cons] at hxmem
    rcases hxmem with rfl | hxmem
    · exact head_ih
    · exact tail_ih x hxmem

I don't quite understand what you mean by "recursion" and "induction". For me, "recursion" is a method for defining functions on inductive types and "induction" is a method for proving properties of such functions. What do you mean when you write "recursion has good support and can do a lot more than induction"?

Anyway, I created an issue in #tpil: https://github.com/leanprover/theorem_proving_in_lean4/issues/229

Oh well with the propositions as types duality, recursion and induction are essentially interchangeable concepts. So proofs that use induction can also be written recursively, e.g. List.append_assoc:

theorem List.append_assoc' (l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α) : (l₁ ++ l₂) ++ l₃ = l₁ ++ (l₂ ++ l₃) := by
  match l₁ with
  | [] => rw [List.nil_append, List.nil_append]
  | x :: t => rw [List.cons_append, List.cons_append, List.cons_append, List.append_assoc']

You can do essentially the same thing for nested inductives.

Also if you want a definition of recursion and induction as I understand it, induction means applying an induction principle while recursion means having a definition or theorem refer to itself (or more generally, a theorem/definition in the same mutual block) within its body.

And an induction principle is essentially a definition or theorem with a type of the following shape:

∀ {param : ...} ...,
∀ {motive : ... → Sort _} ...,
∀ (minor : ... → motive ...) ...,
∀ (major : ...) ...,
motive major ...

or, in words, we have

  • parameters, which can essentially just be anything
  • motives, which describe the type of the result given the object of interest (so usually, what you want to prove about a particular thing)
  • minor premises, whose conclusion is an application of a motive. These are the individual cases of the induction principle and correspond to constructors for an inductive type. If a minor premise takes in arguments that depend on a motive, we call these induction hypotheses.
  • major premises, which can only depend on parameters

and the conclusion is another application of a motive that contains all major premises as arguments. The simplest example of an induction principle is induction on Nat, that is, Nat.rec:

Nat.rec
  -- no parameters
  {motive : Nat → Sort u} -- one motive
  (zero : motive Nat.zero) -- first minor premise
  (succ : (n : Nat) → (n_ih : motive n) → motive n.succ) -- second minor premise
  (t : Nat) : -- one major premise
  motive t -- conclusion

our nested VTree also has an induction principle (two in fact):

VTree.rec
  {α : Type u} -- one parameter
  {motive_1 : VTree α → Sort u_1} -- first motive
  {motive_2 : List (VTree α) → Sort u_1} -- second motive
  -- three minor premises
  (mk : (val : α) → (kids : List (VTree α)) → motive_2 kids → motive_1 { val := val, kids := kids })
  (nil : motive_2 [])
  (cons : (head : VTree α) → (tail : List (VTree α)) → motive_1 head → motive_2 tail → motive_2 (head :: tail))
  (t : VTree α) : -- one major premise
  motive_1 t -- conclusion

The other one is VTree.rec_1 which has motive_2 as a conclusion. The reason induction has trouble here is that it is easy to infer the motive based on the goal state if you just have one motive. But VTree.rec has two motives! So if you have your goal state about VTree, the induction tactic can't know what you want to prove about lists of VTrees.

And if you think about what an induction principle is; it's essentially a recursive case split: without the induction hypotheses, what an induction principle does is it lets you prove a general statement (for any major premises) using individual cases (minor premises, which instead have concrete arguments for the motive). And then the induction hypotheses essentially give you another recursive case split on a part of the arguments of the minor premise.

OK, I guess one way to put it is to say that an induction principle is a recursive function that builds up a proof of a property about an object from sub-proofs of the same property about its constituent sub-objects. This takes advantage of the fact that proofs are first-class objects in Lean (propositions = types implies that proofs are also objects in types).

Anyway, have you considered writing the above up as an addition to #tpil or a Lean community blog post or a chapter in Mathlib Phrasebook? I suspect I'm not the first and only person who needs the above tutorial.
